text:
The journey of a load across a suspension bridge begins on the deck, where the combined weight of vehicles, pedestrians, and the roadway itself creates a continuous downward pull. Because the deck is suspended in midair across a vast expanse, it is too thin to support this weight on its own. Instead, a rigid framework of steel trusses or aerodynamic box girders beneath the pavement spreads concentrated weights, such as a heavy truck, across a wider area to prevent localized sagging. From the outer edges of this stiffened deck, the downward force transfers immediately into dozens of vertical steel ropes called suspenders. Pulled taut by the weight below, the suspenders carry the load upward purely through tension.

At their upper ends, the vertical suspenders clamp onto the bridge’s defining feature: the sweeping main cables. Constructed from thousands of parallel, high-strength steel wires bound tightly together, these massive cables collect the individual tugs of every suspender along the span. Because a flexible cable cannot resist bending, it naturally drapes into a smooth curve that allows it to carry the entire burden of the bridge through axial tension. Every pound of downward gravity acting on the deck becomes an immense pulling force running along the length of the main cables.

As the main cables sweep upward from the center of the bridge, they reach the peaks of the tall vertical towers, resting in heavy, curved metal grooves known as saddles. Because the cables pull downward on both sides of each tower—weighed down by the main span over the water and pulled taut by the side spans toward the shore—their tension presses straight down onto the saddles. This clever geometry converts the pulling force of the cables into a vertical squeezing force called compression. The towers act as colossal pillars, absorbing millions of pounds of compression and channeling it straight down through their hollow steel or concrete legs. At the base of the towers, massive concrete piers sunk deep into the riverbed receive this vertical push and transfer it safely into the underlying bedrock.

While the towers support the vertical weight of the bridge, they cannot stop the ends of the main cables from slipping inward toward the water. To hold the cables taut, they continue past the towers, sloping down to the shorelines to enter immense structures called anchorages. Inside each anchorage, the thick main cables splay outward into hundreds of individual wire strands, which loop around steel eyebars embedded deep within the structure. In soft ground, an anchorage consists of a colossal block of concrete weighing tens of thousands of tons, using sheer dead weight and ground friction to resist the inward and upward pull of the cables. Where coastal geology permits, engineers instead tunnel the anchorages directly into solid cliffside rock. By locking the cable ends permanently in place, the anchorages bleed the bridge's massive horizontal tension harmlessly into the earth, completing the transfer of weight from the suspended roadway to the unyielding ground.
